name: Triangle side
seoTitle: Triangle side Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Triangle side: work out your result from the A and the B. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
Supply the A, the B and the C and the Triangle side calculator solves for the answer. It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm.

The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Triangle side calculator work?
sections.html:
The Triangle side calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the given, the option and the angle selection); then you type in a (Two sides and perimeter), the b (Two sides and perimeter), the c (Two sides and perimeter) and the α (Angle and two sides).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Triangle side calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Α=(((1 ÷ 2) × (-(A ^ 2) + (B ^ 2) + (C ^ 2)) ÷ (B × C)))
Β=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((A ^ 2) − (B ^ 2) + (C ^ 2)) ÷ (A × C)))
Γ=(((1 ÷ 2) × ((A ^ 2) + (B ^ 2) − (C ^ 2)) ÷ (A × B)))
C=B × the cosine of (Α) + the square root of ((A ^ 2) − (B ^ 2) × (the sine of (Α), 2))
C=A × the cosine of (Β) + the square root of (-(A ^ 2) × (the sine of (Β), 2) + (B ^ 2))
A=B × the cosine of (Γ) + the square root of (-(B ^ 2) × (the sine of (Γ), 2) + (C ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Given set to side and 2 angles, Option set to two angles + side between (ASA), Angle selection set to α and c = 30 cm. The calculator returns a = 15.2314 cm, b = 15.2314 cm, γ = 160 deg and c = 30 cm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: a = 15.2314 cm, b = 15.2314 cm, γ = 160 deg and c = 30 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Given set to side and 2 angles and Option set to two angles + side between (ASA).

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Triangle side calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the A, the B and the C — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Triangle side calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the A, the B and the C, which is 21 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter a (Two sides and perimeter) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. A (Two sides and perimeter) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports a = 15.2314 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Triangle side calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
